origin.text: Leo asked his neighbour to lend him a ladder on Saturday. She smiled and said, “I am afraid it is a little awkward this weekend, but I will see what I can do.” She did not mention another day.

He praised the plan but offered no other date.

He asked the writer to send the invitation again in writing.

feedback.es: Elogia el plan, pero no propone otra fecha ni se compromete: esa ausencia de alternativa es la pista de un rechazo cortés.

origin.audio: When I invited my colleague to the company picnic, he said that it sounded lovely and that he would like to come in principle, but that the weekend was a little difficult for him. I waited for him to suggest another date, but he only smiled and asked about the weather. Later I realised that he had turned me down, as politely as possible.

The writer asks the client for a new deadline.
The writer disagrees politely with the proposal.
The writer changes her mind because of the client's pressure.

feedback.es: «With respect» anuncia el desacuerdo y «I wonder whether» lo suaviza; proponer hablar el lunes es cortesía, no aceptación.

origin.text: With respect, I am not sure that moving the deadline is the best option. I appreciate the client's pressure, but I wonder whether the team has enough time to do the work well. Perhaps we could discuss it on Monday.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Un rechazo con tacto deja la puerta abierta a otro día.»

feedback.es: El sujeto es a tactful refusal; leaves the door open expresa que se ofrece una alternativa.

prompt.es: Escucha el relato: ¿qué aprende quien narra sobre los elogios en inglés?

choices.text: That managers in London reject ideas without ever saying why.
That people in London rarely mean what they say to strangers.
That a neighbour's vague invitation is best taken at face value.
That polite praise can hide doubt, so tone and context matter.

feedback.es: «Brave» sonaba a elogio, pero en ese tono significaba «probablemente un error»: aprendió a escuchar lo que no se dice, sin concluir que nadie habla en serio.

origin.audio: When I first moved to London, I kept a list of phrases that confused me. My manager's “I will think about it” meant no. A neighbour's “we must have a drink sometime” was just goodbye. The worst was a colleague who called mine a very “brave” idea. I thanked him warmly, went home happy and spent the weekend developing it. On Monday my manager quietly removed it from the agenda. Only then did a friend explain that brave, in that tone, means “probably a mistake”. Since then I listen to what people do not say as carefully as to what they do.

prompt.es: ¿Qué quiere decir en realidad quien escribe este correo?

The proposal may be accepted when the company's priorities change.
The writer wants Jordan to rewrite it for another department next year.
The writer is asking him to wait a few more weeks.

feedback.es: «Somewhere» y «elsewhere» lo sitúan fuera de su empresa, y pedirle que no invierta más tiempo es el rechazo definitivo con cortesía.

origin.text: Dear Jordan, thank you for the proposal. I can see that a great deal of work went into it, and I am sure it will find a good home somewhere. At the moment, however, our priorities lie elsewhere, and I would not want you to spend more time on it on our account. I hope that we can keep in touch.

choices.text: The writer finds the soft style dishonest and avoids English speakers whenever possible.
The writer now reads the soft style as courtesy, though clarity is still preferred.
The writer has copied the indirect style and dislikes clear answers.

feedback.es: Ya no cree que una respuesta suave sea una mentira, pero sigue prefiriendo la claridad: comprensión sin adoptar el estilo.

origin.text: In my country, a direct “no” is a sign of honesty. In England I learnt to hear something else in “perhaps”. It took me a year to see that nobody was being dishonest; they were protecting the relationship, not hiding the truth. I still prefer a clear answer, but I no longer think that a soft one is a lie.

prompt.es: Ordena: «No mentían; estaban siendo diplomáticos.»

answer.text: They were not lying; they were being tactful

feedback.es: Were being + adjetivo describe una actitud del momento: tactful explica por qué la respuesta era suave.

Probably: she will confirm as soon as she finishes work.

feedback.es: Elogia el plan pero no se compromete, no da fecha y no propone otra ocasión: es un rechazo cortés, no un sí aplazado.

Some people there are sometimes late, but they always apologise.
People there tend to be late, and many do not apologise.

feedback.es: Tend to y many sustituyen a everybody, always y nobody: la versión conserva la observación sin convertirla en ley.

hint.es: Busca la versión sin todos, siempre ni nadie.

origin.text: A student wrote in her travel blog: “Everybody in that city is always late, and nobody ever apologises.” Her teacher underlined the absolute words and asked for a more careful version.

answer.text: It is not unusual for people to eat late

feedback.es: It is not unusual for + sujeto + to + verbo base: «no es raro que» con sujeto propio.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué defecto tiene la afirmación del hermano?

choices.text: It describes the north with too many exceptions.
It depends on one conversation with a taxi driver.
It generalises from a tiny sample to everybody.
It ignores that waiters are often reserved.

feedback.es: Cuatro personas no representan a todo un lugar: el error está en pasar de una muestra mínima a un «all» absoluto.

origin.audio: After a week in the north, my brother came back saying that all the locals were cold. I asked him how many he had actually spoken to. Four, he admitted: a taxi driver, two waiters and a man in a queue. I told him that four people do not make a nation, and that he could safely say only that the people he met had been rather reserved.

prompt.es: Lee el párrafo: ¿qué postura mantiene quien escribe?

choices.text: Every statement about teenagers is unfair and should be avoided.
Teenagers sleep late because they are lazy and tired.
The habit of sleeping late is the same in every family.
A general pattern is acceptable if it admits exceptions.

feedback.es: Acepta el patrón («tend to»), pero rechaza que valga para todos: la versión segura dice «many» y reconoce la variación.

origin.text: Teachers often say that teenagers tend to sleep late, and this is mostly true. But it is not true of all teenagers, and I know several who are awake at six. The safest statement is that many teenagers prefer later hours, and that the habit varies from one family to another.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Con pocas excepciones, aquí la gente suele ser puntual.»

answer.text: With few exceptions, people here tend to be punctual
accepted: With few exceptions, people here tend to be punctual

feedback.es: With few exceptions puede abrir o cerrar la frase; tend to va seguido de un verbo base (be).

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿cuál es la postura de la investigadora sobre las generalizaciones?

choices.text: It is fair to notice a pattern, but wrong to present it as a rule with no exceptions.
Travellers should avoid forming any impression of a country from one visit.
Tiredness explains why some people are unfriendly, so the pattern is fair.
Exceptions should be ignored, because they rarely change anybody's mind.

feedback.es: No condena observar patrones, sino convertirlos en ley: propone generalizar dejando espacio a las excepciones.

origin.audio: A researcher interviewed on a podcast recently described what she calls the airport effect. A traveller spends two hours in a foreign airport, meets three tired officials and decides that the whole country is unfriendly. The mistake, she says, is not in noticing a pattern, but in announcing it as a law. By and large, she added, people tend to be helpful when they are not exhausted. If you must generalise, leave room for the exceptions, because the exceptions are usually the people who change your mind. Her listeners laughed, but many wrote in afterwards to say that they had been guilty of the airport effect themselves.

prompt.es: ¿Qué objeta en realidad quien escribe la carta a la reseña?

choices.text: The mention that some residents are shy with strangers.
The use of absolute words where a hedge would be accurate.
The fact that the reviewer was a stranger to the town.
The claim that a few restaurants close early.

feedback.es: Admite que hay gente tímida y restaurantes que cierran pronto: lo que rechaza son never y every, donde most habría sido exacto.

origin.text: Your review of our town claims that the locals never smile and that every restaurant closes at nine. I have lived here for forty years. Many people are shy with strangers, and a few restaurants do close early, but the words never and every spoil an otherwise fair piece. A reviewer who wrote most would have been accurate, and I would not be writing this letter.

prompt.es: Completa: «Con pocas excepciones, los vecinos llegan a tiempo.»

answer.text: exceptions

feedback.es: With few exceptions es la colocación que matiza una generalización sin abandonarla.

origin.text: Nobody can say that every neighbour is punctual, but with few ___, the people on my street arrive on time and apologise when they are late.

prompt.es: Matiza la frase con una estructura de tendencia (tend to, by and large…).

origin.text: When people say that all young people are impatient, I think of my grandfather, who demanded his dinner at six sharp every evening. Being impatient is not a problem of one age; it is a human habit, and it tends to appear in every age group. I would gladly replace all with many, and then we could start an honest conversation.

origin.audio: An exchange student from Japan told us that in her country it is polite to refuse a second helping once or twice. In her host family's home, she refused twice and went to bed hungry, because nobody offered a third time. The next morning, her host mother explained that here a refusal is taken at face value. They laughed about it, and since then the family has learned to insist a little, while the student has learned to say yes.

prompt.es: Lee el caso: ¿por qué se sintió avergonzada Sara?

choices.text: Her polite phrase was understood literally.
Her host had not offered her any food.
She had eaten more than the family expected.
Her host thought that she was being rude.

feedback.es: Sara solo quería decir que estaba casi llena y el anfitrión lo entendió al pie de la letra: hubo dos supuestos, no mala educación.

origin.text: When Sara thanked her host by saying that she would not eat anything else, he took her at her word and cleared the plates. Sara, who had meant that she was almost full, felt embarrassed. Nobody was rude; both had simply assumed that the other used words in the same way.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Nadie quiso hacer daño, pero suponían cosas distintas.»

answer.text: Nobody meant any harm, but they assumed different things

feedback.es: Nobody meant any harm separa la intención del resultado; but introduce el contraste con assumed different things.

prompt.es: Escucha el relato: ¿qué supuesto tenía la familia sobre Marta?

choices.text: That she disliked the food that the family usually cooked for guests.
That she was unhappy or shy, since she never opened the fridge.
That she expected the mother to serve her every meal.
That she was used to eating alone in her own room.

feedback.es: Cada lado suponía algo distinto: Marta esperaba que le ofrecieran comida; la familia creyó que era tímida o infeliz por no abrir la nevera.

origin.audio: Last spring, Marta, an exchange student from Chile, stayed with a family in Leeds. On her first evening, the father told her to help herself to anything in the kitchen. Marta, who had been raised to wait until food is offered, thanked him and stayed hungry until breakfast. The family, in turn, noticed that she never opened the fridge and assumed that she was unhappy or shy. Only after a week did the mother say, over tea, that in their house guests are expected to serve themselves, and that asking is not needed. Marta burst out laughing, and so did everyone else. From then on, the fridge became the centre of their conversations.

prompt.es: ¿Qué reacción le conviene más a Tom la próxima vez, según el caso?

choices.text: Tell his manager that the colleague had been rude to him during the meeting.
Stop presenting proposals to colleagues from other countries.
Ask what the next step is before reporting an approval.
Insist until the colleague finally answers yes or no in plain words.

feedback.es: Preguntar con tacto por el siguiente paso evita suponer un sí; acusar, rendirse o forzar una respuesta directa ignora que el colega quiso evitar la vergüenza.

origin.text: Tom's Japanese colleague smiled slightly and said that Tom's proposal was very interesting, then changed the subject. Tom left the meeting pleased and told his manager that the idea had been approved. A week later he learned that the colleague had meant that the proposal could not go ahead. The colleague felt that a direct refusal would have embarrassed them both.

prompt.es: Completa: «Puede dar la impresión de ser tímido.»

answer.text: across

feedback.es: Come across as describe la impresión que causa alguien, que puede no coincidir con su intención real.

origin.text: A guest who never speaks during dinner may come ___ as shy, although in his family silence is a sign of respect.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada situación con el supuesto que la explica.

pairs: A guest arrives at eight for a dinner planned for six

pairs.es: supuesto sobre la hora de la cena

pairs: A student keeps her shoes on where everybody takes them off

pairs.es: supuesto sobre los zapatos dentro de casa

pairs: A manager says “We will see” and the visitor hears a yes

pairs.es: supuesto sobre el sentido de una frase cortés

pairs: A host stays silent at dinner and the student thinks he is angry

pairs.es: supuesto sobre el significado del silencio

feedback.es: En cada caso nadie fue maleducado: dos personas aplicaron reglas distintas a la misma situación.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la postura de quien escribe la columna sobre los malentendidos?

choices.text: Travel makes people more open in almost every case.
Bad manners are the main cause of trouble between countries.
Guests should wait patiently and let hosts explain their customs.
Asking questions beats simply being patient.

feedback.es: Considera que la paciencia no basta y propone preguntar antes de juzgar; el origen del problema es suponer que nuestras costumbres son universales.

origin.text: We like to think that travel opens the mind, yet most misunderstandings come from a simple failure to think. We assume that our habits are the normal setting everywhere, and when a host acts differently, we explain it as bad manners. Curiosity, not patience, is the better response: ask first, judge later.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Concede a tu anfitrión el beneficio de la duda.»

answer.text: Give your host the benefit of the doubt

feedback.es: Give + persona + the benefit of the doubt: el anfitrión va antes de la expresión fija.

prompt.es: Escucha el mensaje: ¿qué quiere aclarar Sara a Marta?

choices.text: That “we will see” was a refusal, not a promise.
That Sunday is the best day for a family dinner.
That Marta should ask before accepting an invitation.
That her family always says no to every invitation.

feedback.es: Sara explica que su «we would see» era un no cortés, reconoce que debió decirlo con claridad y pide que no se haya ofendido.

origin.audio: Hello Marta, it is Sara. I am sorry about last night. When I told you that we would see about Sunday, I did not mean yes. In my family that is a polite no. I should have said so clearly, and I hope that you did not take offence.

title.en: Explain a custom to a visitor
title.es: Explicar una costumbre a un visitante

es: Explicar una costumbre familiar a un visitante con generalizaciones matizadas, un ejemplo concreto y una comparación respetuosa.

teaching.en: Our Sunday lunch is an old custom and a long-standing tradition, and relatives tend to arrive around noon.
teaching.es: Nuestro almuerzo del domingo es una vieja costumbre y una tradición de larga data, y los parientes suelen llegar hacia el mediodía.
teaching.explanationEs: Se presenta la costumbre y se matiza con tend to.
segments: Our Sunday lunch is an old custom and a
long-standing tradition, and relatives tend to arrive around noon.
teaching.audioText: Our Sunday lunch is an old custom and a long-standing tradition, and relatives tend to arrive around noon.

teaching.en: By and large, a visitor is welcome at our table without an invitation, and a warm welcome is part of the custom.
teaching.es: En general, un visitante es bienvenido en nuestra mesa sin invitación, y una cálida bienvenida forma parte de la costumbre.
teaching.explanationEs: Generalización matizada: «en general», no «siempre».
segments: By and large, a visitor is welcome at our table without
an invitation, and a warm welcome is part of the custom.
teaching.audioText: By and large, a visitor is welcome at our table without an invitation, and a warm welcome is part of the custom.

teaching.en: For example, we all share one big dish from the centre of the table as a gesture of hospitality.
teaching.es: Por ejemplo, todos compartimos un plato grande del centro de la mesa como gesto de hospitalidad.
teaching.explanationEs: For example introduce un ejemplo concreto que ilustra la costumbre.
segments: For example, we all share one big dish from the
centre of the table as a gesture of hospitality.
teaching.audioText: For example, we all share one big dish from the centre of the table as a gesture of hospitality.

teaching.en: Some cultures serve separate plates, whereas in mine the shared dish may strike a visitor as unusual at first.
teaching.es: Algunas culturas sirven platos separados, mientras que en la mía el plato compartido puede parecerle inusual a un visitante al principio.
teaching.explanationEs: Whereas contrasta dos costumbres sin juzgar ninguna.
segments: Some cultures serve separate plates, whereas in mine the shared
dish may strike a visitor as unusual at first.
teaching.audioText: Some cultures serve separate plates, whereas in mine the shared dish may strike a visitor as unusual at first.

teaching.en: A custom that is second nature to us is easy to overlook, but a visitor notices it at once.
teaching.es: Una costumbre que para nosotros es algo natural es fácil de pasar por alto, pero un visitante la nota de inmediato.
teaching.explanationEs: Lo automático para unos es lo llamativo para otros.
segments: A custom that is second nature to us is easy
to overlook, but a visitor notices it at once.
teaching.audioText: A custom that is second nature to us is easy to overlook, but a visitor notices it at once.

teaching.en: In many households it is customary to bring a small gift, and the host will share the best seat with a guest.
teaching.es: En muchas casas es costumbre llevar un pequeño regalo, y el anfitrión comparte el mejor asiento con el invitado.
teaching.explanationEs: It is customary to + verbo base: «es costumbre» sin culpar a nadie.
segments: In many households it is customary to bring a small gift,
and the host will share the best seat with a guest.
teaching.audioText: In many households it is customary to bring a small gift, and the host will share the best seat with a guest.

prompt.es: ¿Cómo debería corregir la estudiante esta explicación de su costumbre?

choices.text: In my country we eat at ten, which is obviously the only correct time for dinner.
In my country eating at six is strange, so you should really change your habit.
In my country nobody ever eats at six, unlike all other countries.
In my country families tend to eat at ten, whereas in yours it is earlier.

feedback.es: Tend to matiza la generalización y whereas contrasta sin juzgar; las demás versiones elogian la propia costumbre o rechazan la ajena.

hint.es: Busca la versión que describe la diferencia sin decir cuál es mejor.

origin.text: A student is describing the dinner time in her family: “In my country everybody eats dinner at ten, which is much better than the silly habit of eating at six.” Her teacher asks for a version that a visitor could hear without feeling hurt.

prompt.es: Completa: «El plato compartido puede parecerle inusual a un visitante.»

answer.text: strike

feedback.es: Strike someone as + adjetivo describe la impresión que algo causa a una persona, sin juzgar lo que es.

hint.es: Verbo que significa «golpear», pero aquí describe una impresión.

origin.text: In my house everybody shares one big dish, and this may ___ a visitor as unusual at first, although by the end of the evening it seems natural.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Ninguna forma es mejor porque cada costumbre tiene sentido en casa.»

answer.text: Neither way is better because each custom makes sense at home

feedback.es: Neither way is better + because + causa: la comparación respetuosa explica por qué no hay un ganador.

hint.es: Empieza con neither way y termina con at home.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué actitud tiene quien narra hacia la costumbre de su abuela?

choices.text: It moves the narrator, although the cousins consider it odd.
It moves the narrator, and the cousins feel exactly the same.
It seems strange to the narrator, as it does to the cousins.
It worries the narrator whenever a visitor asks about it.

feedback.es: Contrasta con whereas: sus primos la consideran rara, pero a quien narra le emociona porque recuerda que la bienvenida no termina en la puerta.

origin.audio: My grandmother has a custom that surprises every visitor: before anyone eats, she puts a little food on a small plate by the window. She says it is a gesture of hospitality for anyone who might be passing. Whereas my cousins find it odd, I find it moving, because it reminds me that a welcome does not end at the front door.

prompt.es: Lee la situación: ¿qué frase compara dos costumbres con respeto?

choices.text: In my family we tend to sing first, which is obviously the correct way.
In my family we tend to sing first, whereas in many countries people cut the cake first.
In other countries people tend to cut the cake first, whereas we do it the right way.
Everybody in my family always sings first, unlike all other countries.

feedback.es: Tend to y whereas describen la diferencia sin juicio; las otras opciones, aunque usen las mismas estructuras, declaran una costumbre correcta o universal.

origin.text: A student is explaining to an exchange student how her family celebrates birthdays. She wants to describe the difference without sounding better than anybody else, and she is looking for the best sentence to use.

prompt.es: Ordena: «En general, los visitantes son bienvenidos a nuestra mesa.»

answer.text: By and large, visitors are welcome at our table

feedback.es: By and large abre la frase y matiza; visitors are welcome at our table es la generalización.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué quiere transmitir quien habla al describir las costumbres de su casa?

choices.text: That visitors should copy her customs as soon as they arrive.
That her mother's kitchen rules are stricter than other families' rules.
That habits which look odd are gestures of welcome with their own logic.
That cooking together is a better custom than cooking alone.

feedback.es: Cada hábito que sorprende resulta ser un gesto de bienvenida con su lógica; la comparación final, «neither way is better», evita juzgar.

origin.audio: When visitors first come to my house, they usually notice three things: the shoes by the door, the very long goodbye and the fact that my mother will not let anyone help in the kitchen. At first glance these habits may strike them as strange. By and large, however, they leave understanding that each one is a gesture of welcome: the shoes keep the floor clean for the children, the long goodbye shows that nobody is in a hurry, and the empty kitchen is my mother's way of saying that a guest is a guest. Whereas in my friend's home everybody cooks together, in ours the cook is the host. Neither way is better; both are ways of saying: you matter.

prompt.es: ¿Qué corrección propone quien revisa el borrador?

choices.text: Delete the shared dish example because it is too personal.
Remove every comparison with other countries from the paragraph.
Soften “cold” to “a bit cold” so that the generalisation sounds fairer.
Replace the judgement by a description of behaviour.

feedback.es: Elogia el ejemplo y el tono cálido, pero el juicio «cold» sobre otras personas debe sustituirse por lo que hacen: describir conductas, no rasgos.

origin.text: Your paragraph about Sunday lunch is warm and vivid, and the example of the shared dish works well. However, the sentence “In other countries people are cold at meals” is an unfair generalisation, and it undermines the respectful tone of the rest. A better comparison would describe what people do, not what they are.

prompt.es: Completa: «En algunas casas es costumbre quitarse los zapatos al entrar.»

answer.text: customary

feedback.es: It is customary to + verbo base es la fórmula de registro más formal para «es costumbre».

origin.text: Guests do not always know the rules of a new house, but in some homes it is ___ to take off your shoes at the door, and a polite visitor does it without being asked.

prompt.es: Explica una costumbre de tu familia a un visitante (180–240 palabras).

answer.text: In my family, Friday dinner is a long-standing tradition. By and large, everybody is home by seven, and the children tend to choose the menu. For example, last week my little brother asked for rice and chicken, and we all agreed. A visitor is always welcome, and guests usually bring a dessert or a small gift. It is customary to share one big dish from the centre of the table, which may strike a visitor as unusual at first. In many countries each person has a separate plate, whereas in mine we pass the food around and talk while we eat. Neither way is better; each custom makes sense at home. Please do not worry if you are unsure what to do: my mother will show you, and she will give you a warm welcome. I hope that you can join us one Friday.
accepted: In my family, Friday dinner is a long-standing tradition. By and large, everybody is home by seven, and the children tend to choose the menu. For example, last week my little brother asked for rice and chicken, and we all agreed. A visitor is always welcome, and guests usually bring a dessert or a small gift. It is customary to share one big dish from the centre of the table, which may strike a visitor as unusual at first. In many countries each person has a separate plate, whereas in mine we pass the food around and talk while we eat. Neither way is better; each custom makes sense at home. Please do not worry if you are unsure what to do: my mother will show you, and she will give you a warm welcome. I hope that you can join us one Friday.

Every Sunday my family has lunch at my grandmother's house, a custom that is older than I am. As a rule, everybody arrives around noon, and the younger cousins tend to arrive last. For instance, last month my uncle brought a cake that he had baked himself, and we all laughed because it was still warm. Visitors are welcome too, and they usually sit next to my grandmother. In some countries people eat quickly and leave, whereas in mine the table is a place to stay and talk for hours. Neither way is wrong; each custom simply suits its own home. It may seem unusual at first, but guests quickly feel at ease. I would love to see you there one Sunday.

feedback.es: Un texto completo presenta la costumbre, matiza dos generalizaciones, da un ejemplo concreto y compara con respeto, sin juzgar.

origin.text: Explica a un visitante extranjero una costumbre de tu familia (la cena del viernes, el almuerzo del domingo…). Escribe en inglés con dos generalizaciones matizadas (by and large, tend to…), un ejemplo concreto y una comparación respetuosa con otra costumbre.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la postura de quien escribe sobre explicar una costumbre a un extraño?

choices.text: Explaining a custom values it and welcomes strangers.
Explaining a custom makes it sound less natural, so it is best avoided.
Only customs that are very old deserve an explanation.
Strangers should learn the customs without asking questions.

feedback.es: Rebate la idea del museo: explicar con cariño mantiene viva la costumbre y abre la puerta al extraño.

origin.text: Some people claim that explaining a custom to a stranger makes it sound less natural, as if we were showing our family in a museum. I see it differently. A custom that we cannot explain is one that we have stopped noticing, and describing it kindly is a way of keeping it alive and of inviting the stranger in.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Mientras que nosotros compartimos un plato, ellos usan platos separados.»

answer.text: Whereas we share one dish, they use separate plates
accepted: Whereas we share one dish, they use separate plates
They use separate plates, whereas we share one dish

feedback.es: Whereas une dos hechos contrastados; puede abrir la frase o ir en medio, separado por coma.

prompt.es: Escucha el mensaje: ¿qué actitud muestra Ana al explicar la costumbre?

choices.text: Formal: she lists conditions that Tom must accept to be welcome.
Relaxed and welcoming: she explains a habit, not a demand.
Nervous: she worries that Tom will dislike her family's customs.
Defensive: she justifies her family's habits before Tom can judge them.

feedback.es: Dice «not a rule, just a habit» y ofrece una solución si olvida algo: explica una costumbre con calidez y sin imponerla.

origin.audio: Hi Tom, it is Ana. About Saturday: at our house we tend to take off our shoes at the door, so bring some warm socks. It is not a rule, just a habit, and my mother will lend you some if you forget. She would be very happy if you tried her dessert, which is an old family recipe.

title.en: Host a guest, avoid the clash
title.es: Recibir a un invitado sin choques

es: Recibir a un invitado extranjero: explicar dos costumbres con matices, aclarar un malentendido con tacto y responder a una pregunta incómoda.

vocabulary.es: no quise decir, no era mi intención

teaching.en: Please feel at home: a guest who is afraid to open the fridge will never relax, however kind the welcome.
teaching.es: Siéntete como en casa: un invitado que tiene miedo de abrir la nevera nunca se relajará, por amable que sea la bienvenida.
teaching.explanationEs: Feel at home es una bienvenida cálida que da permiso al invitado.
segments: Please feel at home: a guest who is afraid to
open the fridge will never relax, however kind the welcome.
teaching.audioText: Please feel at home: a guest who is afraid to open the fridge will never relax, however kind the welcome.

teaching.en: If a misunderstanding has spoiled the evening, apologise briefly and tactfully, without blaming the guest.
teaching.es: Si un malentendido ha estropeado la velada, discúlpate con brevedad y con tacto, sin culpar al invitado.
teaching.explanationEs: Apologise reconoce un fallo sin dramatizar; se dice apologise for…
segments: If a misunderstanding has spoiled the evening, apologise
briefly and tactfully, without blaming the guest.
teaching.audioText: If a misunderstanding has spoiled the evening, apologise briefly and tactfully, without blaming the guest.

teaching.en: Let me clarify: we did not mean to ignore you when we started eating, because in our house nobody waits after seven.
teaching.es: Déjame aclarar: no queríamos ignorarte cuando empezamos a comer, porque en nuestra casa nadie espera después de las siete.
teaching.explanationEs: Clarify + did not mean: aclara la intención sin culpar a nadie.
segments: Let me clarify: we did not mean to ignore you when
we started eating, because in our house nobody waits after seven.
teaching.audioText: Let me clarify: we did not mean to ignore you when we started eating, because in our house nobody waits after seven.

teaching.en: When the guest asks an awkward question, say “Good question” and tread carefully: answer honestly, but without absolute words.
teaching.es: Cuando el invitado hace una pregunta incómoda, di «Buena pregunta» y ve con cuidado: responde con honestidad, pero sin palabras absolutas.
teaching.explanationEs: Reconocer lo delicado y responder sin «siempre» ni «nunca» evita una discusión.
segments: When the guest asks an awkward question, say “Good question”
and tread carefully: answer honestly, but without absolute words.
teaching.audioText: When the guest asks an awkward question, say “Good question” and tread carefully: answer honestly, but without absolute words.

teaching.en: To clear the air after a clash, set the record straight about your custom and invite the guest to ask anything.
teaching.es: Para despejar el ambiente tras un choque, aclara las cosas sobre tu costumbre e invita al invitado a preguntar lo que quiera.
teaching.explanationEs: Clear the air y set the record straight buscan reparar, no ganar.
segments: To clear the air after a clash, set the record straight
about your custom and invite the guest to ask anything.
teaching.audioText: To clear the air after a clash, set the record straight about your custom and invite the guest to ask anything.

teaching.en: “No offence” is a softener for criticism, so use it sparingly, and never after an awkward remark that has already hurt someone.
teaching.es: «Sin ofender» suaviza una crítica, así que úsalo con moderación y nunca tras un comentario incómodo que ya ha herido a alguien.
teaching.explanationEs: No offence no borra una ofensa: solo suaviza lo que aún no se ha dicho.
segments: “No offence” is a softener for criticism, so use it sparingly,
and never after an awkward remark that has already hurt someone.
teaching.audioText: “No offence” is a softener for criticism, so use it sparingly, and never after an awkward remark that has already hurt someone.

prompt.es: Lee el intercambio: ¿por qué es diplomática la respuesta de Sara?

choices.text: It avoids the question by changing the subject quickly.
It admits that the family is unfriendly to every guest.
It welcomes the question and avoids absolute words.

feedback.es: Sara reconoce la pregunta con «Good question!» y responde con by and large y una razón concreta, sin absolutos ni evasivas.

hint.es: Fíjate en cómo empieza su respuesta y en las palabras que evita.

origin.text: Carlos, a guest from abroad, asks his hosts why nobody talks during dinner. Sara smiles and answers, “Good question! By and large we talk a lot, but tonight we were all very tired.” Carlos laughs, and the silence disappears.

prompt.es: Completa: «Ana preparó té para despejar el ambiente.»

answer.text: air

feedback.es: Clear the air es la expresión fija para disipar la tensión tras una discusión o un malentendido.

origin.text: After the argument at dinner, nobody wanted to speak first, so Ana made tea to clear the ___ between them and offer a fresh start.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada expresión del anfitrión con su función.

pairs: Let me clarify…
No offence, but…
Please feel at home
Good question!

feedback.es: Cada expresión cumple un papel distinto al recibir a un invitado: aclarar, suavizar, acoger y responder con tacto.

hint.es: Piensa en el orden de una visita: bienvenida, malentendido, pregunta.

pairs: Let me clarify…
No offence, but…
Please feel at home
Good question!

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué hizo especialmente bien el padre al contestar a la invitada?

choices.text: He explained the habit but insisted that the guest must follow it.
He explained the habit and offered to adapt it if the guest preferred.
He offered to change the habit without explaining why it exists.
He apologised for the habit and promised to abandon it for good.

feedback.es: Reconoce la pregunta, describe el hábito con «tend to» y se ofrece a adaptarlo: así la invitada se siente en casa.

origin.audio: Our guest from Canada arrived on Friday and asked why we never eat before eight. My father said, “Good question. Most families here tend to eat late, but it is only a habit, and we can eat earlier if you prefer.” The guest looked relieved. She said later that nobody had ever answered her so kindly, and that she felt at home by the end of the evening.

prompt.es: Lee el mensaje: ¿qué busca quien lo escribe?

choices.text: To excuse the family by proving that the guest was in the wrong.
To ask the guest to follow the customs of the house from now on.
To clear the air by explaining the custom kindly.
To cancel the invitation politely without saying so.

feedback.es: Se disculpa, explica la costumbre (la cocinera come la última) y deja la puerta abierta a más preguntas, sin culpar al invitado.

origin.text: I apologise for what happened at dinner. We did not mean to leave you out; in our house the cook eats last and the guests start first, so we assumed that you would begin. Please tell me if anything else surprises you.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Por favor, siéntete como en casa y pregúntame lo que quieras.»

answer.text: Please feel at home and ask me anything

feedback.es: Feel at home es una expresión fija; ask me anything invita al invitado a preguntar sin reservas.

prompt.es: Escucha el relato: ¿cómo arregla la familia la situación con Jamal?

choices.text: By asking Jamal to explain why he had not slept well that night.
By removing the house rules and inviting him to write his own list.
By telling Jamal politely that a second blanket was not really needed.
By saying sorry for the joke, making clear the list was no order and giving him a blanket.

feedback.es: La familia se disculpa por la broma, aclara que la lista no era una orden y ofrece la manta sin comentarios: reparar sin culpar.

origin.audio: When Jamal, an exchange student from Kenya, came to stay with us, my mother gave him a list of house rules, which was the first mistake. The second was my father's joke that only tourists ask for a second blanket. Jamal smiled politely, but the next morning he looked tired. My mother, who reads faces well, took me aside and suggested that we apologise for the joke, clarify that the list was not an order, and offer a blanket without comment. At breakfast my father said, with a smile, that he had been a bad host and a worse performer. Jamal laughed, accepted the blanket, and asked whether the house rules included the recipe for my mother's bread.

prompt.es: ¿Qué busca quien escribe al responder así a la pregunta incómoda de Hana?

choices.text: To reply frankly to a difficult question, limited to what the writer knows.
To avoid the question by praising the families the writer knows.
To prove that every family in the town is quieter than Hana's.
To apologise because the writer's family is so different from Hana's.

feedback.es: Acota («only speak for the families I know»), matiza con «many» y «tend to» y explica sin disculparse: una respuesta sincera y sin absolutos.

origin.text: Dear Hana, you asked whether all the families in our town are as quiet as mine. It is a good question, and I should say first that I can only speak for the families I know. Many of them tend to be reserved at dinner, but others are noisy, particularly on Sundays. Please do not take our quiet as a sign that we are cold; it is simply how we were brought up.

origin.text: I did not mean to be rude when we started eating without you, so let me set the record ___ about what happened last night.

prompt.es: Da la bienvenida a tu invitado, aclara y responde con tacto (200–260 palabras).

answer.text: Welcome, Carlos, and please feel at home! In my family we tend to eat dinner at six, and by and large everybody helps to set the table. Let me clarify something about last night: we did not mean to be rude when we started eating without you. I apologise, because I should have explained that we usually do not wait after seven. You asked a good question: why do we not talk more at dinner? It is a fair thing to wonder, and I will try to answer tactfully. Some families are quieter, and ours likes to enjoy the food first, whereas in your country people seem to talk more. Neither way is better, and it is only a habit; nobody is upset. Tomorrow we will talk as much as you like, and I will show you the city. No offence if we are quiet again on Sunday: my grandmother cooks, and we tend to listen to her stories.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la actitud de quien escribe ante los invitados de otros países?

choices.text: Guests should accept every habit of the host without asking.
Open explanation and questions are better than guessing what offends.
It is wiser to avoid inviting people from other countries.
Hosts should leave every guest alone to avoid any problem.

feedback.es: Ya no adivina qué ofende: explica sus hábitos y pregunta por los del invitado, una estrategia sin coste que evita casi todo el daño.

origin.text: Hosting a foreigner taught me that politeness has no universal grammar. Some guests want to be left alone; others think that being left alone means being ignored. I used to worry that every choice would offend someone. Now I explain my habits openly and ask about theirs, which costs nothing and avoids most of the damage.

feedback.es: Agradece la velada, resta importancia a su respuesta larga y cierra con un proverbio que muestra que se siente a gusto.

origin.audio: Thank you for the lovely evening. Your question about my country was not awkward at all, although I am afraid my answer was too long. Please tell me if I talk too much. Back home we say that a guest who is shy at the start is a guest who will be very happy in the end.
